caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Kenya's debt has doubled as a share of GDP in a decade of infrastructure borrowing. From 34.2% in 2007, the ratio rose steadily as the government issued debut Eurobonds (2014) and borrowed heavily from China for the Standard Gauge Railway: it reached 73.4% in 2023, the series high, easing to a projected 68.9% in 2025. Debt service now consumes a huge share of revenues, and the 2024 maturity of the $2 billion 2014 Eurobond forced a costly refinancing. IMF assessments judge debt sustainable but at high risk of distress; the real constraint is liquidity, not solvency, with markets pricing Kenya as a perpetual refinancing risk.
inflation_management: The Central Bank of Kenya's inflation-targeting framework (5% with a ±2.5 point band) has a mixed record. It failed the early tests: inflation hit 15.1% in 2008 and 14.0% in 2011 on food and currency shocks. But from 2013 the framework gained credibility, keeping inflation mostly within 4-8% for a decade, including through COVID. The 2022-23 global shock pushed it to 7.6-7.7%, just above target, before easing to 4.5% in 2024 and a projected 4.1% in 2025, the series low. The CBK hiked aggressively in 2023-24 and has earned a reputation as one of Africa's more credible central banks, though fiscal dominance remains the background threat.

key_events.event: Disputed election triggered post-election violence; inflation spiked to 15.1%.
New constitution devolved power to 47 counties, reshaping public finance.
Debut $2.75 billion Eurobond; Standard Gauge Railway construction began with Chinese financing.
COVID-19; Kenya received IMF support; debt climbed past 65% of GDP.
William Ruto won the presidential election; debt peaked at 73.4% of GDP.
June 2024: deadly protests forced withdrawal of the Finance Bill's tax hikes; the government refinanced the maturing Eurobond at high cost.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued market-access juggling: Kenya will keep refinancing its way forward with IMF support, inflation near target, and growth around 5%. Upside comes from fiscal consolidation actually sticking; downside is a failed bond auction or political unrest forcing a restructuring. Uncertainty is moderate: Kenya's institutions are resilient, but the debt-service burden leaves no room for policy error.
